en: Coral hat finials, precious coral stones:
Among Konurbai's army
Is the khan of Luntun too.
I pictured them as well:
Khan Zholoi, khan of the lamas;
Orokkyr, khan of the Shibe;
Muzkindik, khan of the Solon;
Ezkara, khan of the Manchu;
Konurbai, the greatest of them all.
Setting them all in an equal row,
I pictured them together.
If you look to your right,
When he faces forward,
He has the look of a lion;
When he turns his back,
He has the dread majesty of six thousand warriors.
Taking the shape of a night terror,
With eyes like a hungry lion's,
With a face like buttered wheat,
With eyes like dusky mist,
His eyes as broad as a lake basin,
As though to swallow all he sees,
Of middling height and broad shoulders:
I dressed him in Akolpok,
I mounted him on Akkula,
Driving back the swarming Chinese,
Making them flee stiff with fear,
Sending them all toward Beijing,
I pictured your father.
Akkula beneath him,
A creature of splendid animal form,
The foal of a young mare,
The Duldul of the horse herds:
'Your father's Akkula—
Let the orphan see him clearly,' I thought,
And pictured him too.
On this side of him,
Tall and broad-shouldered,
Both a champion and a lion,
As great as half a mountain,
As though to devour whoever appeared,
With a white face without freckles,
With sheep-brown eyes, no pale eyes,
Wearing yellow leather trousers,
Riding a horse such as Sarala,
Carrying a spear without a tuft,
A naked sword strapped at his side:
Almambet, son of Khan Azyz,
Was your father's sworn brother;
I pictured him.
Girding his accomplished warrior's waist,
If seven great dark hosts came,
He would plunge in with his coat loose and attack.
On this side of him,
With black felt edging on his hat,
Your own kinsman,
Khan Manas's Syrgak:
Never resting upon his elbow,
Never sleeping so much as a wink,
Light upon a horse, suited to a colt,
Sleepless, watchful on the road,
Bringing good fortune when sent ahead,
Worth a great host when driving foes:
Riding a strong, enduring steed,
Wearing a coat blue as iron,
Strewing the unbelievers dead,
The dark Kalmaks and Chinese,
Driving them stiff with fear:
I pictured Syrgak.
On this side of him,
Riding a horse such as Kokala,
Wearing a blue ribbed-cloth coat,
With shrill cries and fierce battle shouts,
Beyond the whole world's strength to wrestle down,
Beyond a lion's teeth to pierce,
Who had received a letter from the caliph,
Who was also called a mighty conqueror,
Riding a horse no shot could catch,
Wearing a coat no shot could pierce,
His banner fluttering in his hand,
The dark keen steel that drinks blood
Flashing at his wrist,
His apple-like neck stretching out,
His eyes reddening like a lion's,
Girded with gold and rubies,
Sullen, without a smile,
And laid low Kün Jangjung.
Roaring, attacking alone:
Chubak, your father's sworn brother,
I pictured him too.
On this side of him,
Wearing a gray lynx-fur hat,
Brandishing a mottled blue shield,
Attentive to reasoned words,
His mouth rinsed with honey,
His head was divided by leaves,
His feet resting upon a thousand gold pieces,
Finding words when taken unawares,
Finding sight in darkness,
Bringing good fortune when sent ahead,
Worth a great host when riding behind:
The mount beneath him,
Red-maned and gray-maned,
Never tires when ridden scouting,
Never sickens when ridden to the rear.
Khan Bakai's Kok Tulpar:
Riding a horse such as Kok Tulpar,
His eyes shining like the morning star,
His golden crescent gleaming through a haze:
When your father went to Beijing,
The red banner of the Muslims
I placed in warrior Bakai's hand;
The swarming infidels
I had him drive like dark willow branches;
Those who came before him,
I had your champion Khan Bakai strike down.
Your father's sworn brother, the lion
Bakai, I pictured.
If you look nearer this way,
Broad-chested, with young-camel eyes,
With a majestic, spreading breast,
Whetting his dark tongue,
Singing forth before the khan,
Wearing seven different coats,
Knowing the languages of seventy tribes,
With broad jaws and a broad tongue,
His deep throat never faltering,
Finding reasons, knowing words,
A swift orator, skilled in fitting speech,
With a gifted tongue beyond other men,
With a morning-star forehead among men,
The rival of fortunate warriors,
Who had come to your leopard father Manas
Through his good fortune:
Azhybai, son of the Argyn,
The interpreter of the world,
Wearing a white ribbed-cloth coat,
Riding a horse such as Kartkuron.
That brown horse of Azhybai's,
When your father Manas was alive,
Kartkuron, ridden on dispatches,
Around the four corners of the world,
To circle them four times and return:
Kartkuron, ridden to carry news,
Will not let you be taken in a shooting fight;
Will not flag if you ride him into battle;
Will not tire if you ride him scouting.
Unless his lead rope is shortened to a handful,
He will not yield to a determined foe;
Unless true disaster strikes,
He will not let his rider fall to the foe.
Father Kambar, numbered among the unseen:
Kartkuron, whom he would ride into battle,
When he truly lets out a neigh,
No beast would turn its neck away before him.
The king of the horse herds:
When they heard Kartkuron's voice,
The mountain wild asses followed in a line.
Your father, Khan Manas,
Would go to broad Beijing;
Always he would set Kuron
Before the horses he had seized,
To lead them onward.
The rider upon his back,
With a forked beard and a Sart's face,
Azhybai, son of the Argyn khan,
Had quarreled with his father
And come to settle in Talas.
Becoming your father's friend,
He became a choro to Zhakyp's
Only son, Manas.
A star rose from the sky,
With your fierce father, the lion,
He became a friend until Judgment Day.
Taking keen dark steel,
Furious and grim,
I dressed him in shotproof armor,
I mounted him upon Kartkuron;
The Torgut, Chinese and Manchu,
I set Azhybai upon them;
Into the thick battle where blood flowed,
I sent him without drawing back;
Upon the red-tufted Chinese,
I sent him shouting war cries.
He was your father's sworn brother:
I pictured Azhybai.
Khan Yraman's Yrchyuul,
His trouser cord tasseled, with forty sections,
Warrior Shuutu, with a hat like a yurt's roof felt,
Akzholtoi's Tolgochu,
Khan Shygai's darling,
Urumkhan's golden-crowned Muzburchak,
Kyrgylchal, leader of the forty,
Kyyalkhan's valiant one among spearmen,
Warrior Serek, who came from Lower Crimea,
The fierce hero with far-seeing eyes:
All forty were sons of forty khans.
The moon grows dark,
Each had quarreled with his own people
And come to settle in Talas,
Becoming choros to your father, Sultan Manas.
A choro who came without a horse:
For the choro who came without a horse,
With mountain-sheep legs and copper forelegs,
He provided the finest horse to ride.
From the people he had reached,
Your khan father set him apart
And made him known to all.
A choro who came without a coat:
For the choro who came without a coat,
With a golden collar and copper sleeves,
Double mail with links like larks' eyes,
A metal-thread jacket with a broad collar,
Handsome and proof against shots:
He clothed him in the finest coat.
A choro who came without livestock:
Pied-headed horses upon the hills,
Argymaks and swift steeds together,
All exceptional tulpars:
Your royal father, Khan Manas,
Gave each his own allotted share.
For the choro who came without a home,
He chose a white great yurt and settled him inside.
For the choro who came unmarried,
He ascertained his circumstances;
With a thimble mouth and dark eyes,
From among the graceful beauties,
He procured a wife.
Your father's forty choros:
I sent them on holy war against the Chinese;
Into the hands of the forty choros,
I placed forty spears;
I had them wreak a mighty slaughter.
Grasping spears, breaking the ranks,
Those whose hour had come falling to shots,
Drenched in dark blood,
Fighting without retreat:
Your father's forty choros
I pictured in a row.
Before the forty choros,
Their wits utterly scattered:
Of Kakanchyn's Beijing,
I pictured its panic.
Barefoot and bareheaded,
Hurrying and stumbling in confusion,
I pictured their flight.
The spear-bearing Muslims,
Driving in the Chinese:
I pictured them breaking them apart.
Falling this way and that,
The masses of Chinese and Manchu:
I pictured their deaths.
Teeming like ants,
Swarming thicker than mosquitoes:
I pictured the people of Beijing.
